text: So, from the opposition side, we disagree with the fact that we will reduce the qualification of teachers in the area where there's high illiteracy. So we'll start by setting up what qualification is and what high illiteracy means, and then we will give out a point that reducing the qualification will affect both illiterate and literate students in the government paradigms, and also we'll show the mechanism of how to maintain good quality teachers, even though it's an urgent issue to increase the number of teachers. So, let's start with the setup.

We say that qualification includes teacher training, which results in teacher license, but also a university degree, if you are a general teacher, maybe an education major. If you are, for example, a science teacher, maybe some expertise in math or other science fields like physics.

And so, we would also set up high illiteracy rate as being associated with areas where governments are poor or developing countries, but we would want to argue that because of that, qualification is more important because in those areas, as compared to already developed countries, the qualification for teachers are not that perfect. The criteria still needs improvement. So, if we reduce the qualification of teachers further, then it would make the situation worse because you would have less qualified teachers in an already less qualified criteria.

And especially in highly illiterate areas, students would need a lot of help in reading and understanding language and reading and understanding the passage context. So, you would really need a qualified teacher to help teach them. The teacher that put efforts in teaching.

As compared to literate students who already know how to read, the teacher doesn't have to do much in order to help them learn how to read. But if you need a lot of help, then the teacher has to find specific methods that help those students to teach. So, instead of just conventional teaching, like asking the student to stand up and read the passage and see if they can read, they have to make sure that they understand or help create games that make them engage in the teaching or have after school class to help with students who struggle in class to catch up. And so, in order for teachers to do this, you need a very qualified teacher. So, we would argue that reducing the qualification would only make it worse.

Not only for illiterate students, but also for literate students because if the quality of teaching is low, then literate students who are already good, they cannot improve further. If you have a qualified teacher, then you would help improve literate students to be better and also help illiterate students to catch up with the literate students.

The government side might say that it costs a lot for the qualification and it is an urgent issue. But we would say that the government can initially subsidize this program or subsidize to help boost the salary of the teachers in short term so that it can attract a lot of people who are very qualified or who have a degree attracting people to become teachers. So, then that would solve the issue. And afterwards, the government could improve on the policies to help build a good foundation.

And I think the main thing is that education creates a long term product. So, even though the issue is urgent that you need to improve the literacy rate, but because students learn now and then they grow up and the effect will be seen in 10 years. So, I think it's better, although it's an immediate problem, it's better to solve it with a solution that has a long term effect. Because you will see the effect in 10 years as students grow up. And that would also lay a foundation for areas with high illiteracy rate, to reduce the illiteracy rate so that it will not go back to that. It will lay a foundation for developing countries because high illiteracy areas are mostly related to developing countries as well.
